Q: How to securely store a password for a script run every day using a Windows task scheduler? A:

The general approach of dealing with credentials is to avoid them and instead rely on other means to authenticate, such as certificates or Windows authentication.

As you apparently found out yourself, trying to script a single factor authentication either ends up in a catch-22 or isn't secure as everybody that has access to your script has access to the key no matter how deep you try to hide it using security through obscurity.

If you aren't able to change the authentication way of the application, the safest practical way is probably to create your own "single sign-on" in means of using the Windows DPAPI (Data Protection API) where the encryption is based on the computer and the user credentials.

For this you might use the PowerShell ConvertTo-SecureString and ConvertFrom-SecureString cmdlets.
First create a secure string (under the concerned computer/user account):

Read-Host 'Enter your password' -AsSecureString | ConvertFrom-SecureString

This will return a string like:



⚠️ warning
The contents of a SecureString are not encrypted on non-Windows systems.

You might simply put this string in an environment variable or simply embed this in your script or better (as correctly mentioned by Gregory) hide it in a separate file to protect it from event logging:

$EncryptedPassword = '01000000d08c9ddf...

Note that this string can only be decrypted on the specific computer and by the user account that created the $EncryptePassword. This limitation adds in fact the security (also knowing that everytime you use the ConvertFrom-SecureString command you will get a different string).

To reveal the plain text password in your script you might do something like:

$Password = $EncryptedPassword | ConvertTo-SecureString | ConvertFrom-SecureString -AsPlainText

⚠️ warning
Try to avoid disclosing SecureString as a String as it might leave memory (or even log) traces. Therefore it is a good thing to at least remove the decrypted variables, e.g.: Remove-Variable Password.

Encrypting your script

You could even consider to DPAPI encrypt your whole script including hardcoded plain passwords (which actually better secures it than using tools as PS2EXE):

# Protect-Script.ps1

param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory=$true, Position=0, ValueFromPipeline=$true)]
    [string] $Path,
    [switch] $AsBase64
)
$Item = Get-Item $Path
if ($Item) {
    $OutPath = "$($Item.DirectoryName)\$($Item.BaseName).Protected$($Item.Extension)"
    $ScriptBlock = Get-Content -Raw -Path $Path
    $Hex = $ScriptBlock | ConvertTo-SecureString -AsPlainText -Force | ConvertFrom-SecureString
    if ($AsBase64) {
        $Bytes = [byte[]] -split ($Hex -replace '..', '0x$& ')
        $Base64 = [Convert]::ToBase64String($Bytes)
        Set-Content -Path $OutPath "`$Base64 = '$Base64'"
        Add-Content -Path $OutPath '$Bytes = [System.Convert]::FromBase64String($Base64)'
        Add-Content -Path $OutPath '$Hex = -Join $Bytes.Foreach{ $_.ToString("x2") }'
    }
    else {
        Set-Content -Path $OutPath "`$Hex = '$Hex'"
    }
    Add-Content -Path $OutPath '$ScriptBlock = $Hex | ConvertTo-SecureString | ConvertFrom-SecureString -AsPlainText'
    Add-Content -Path $OutPath 'Invoke-Expression $ScriptBlock'
    Add-Content -Path $OutPath 'Remove-Variable Base64, Bytes, Hex, ScriptBlock -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue'
}

Usage:

.\Protect-Script.ps1 .\MailMessage.ps1 -AsBase64

.\MailMessage.Protected.ps1

Again: in essence, the .\MailMessage.Protected.ps1 script will only work (and can only be decrypted) on the computer and under the account were it was created.

(update 2026-01-20)

Sharing a protected script

In case you want to share a protected script (in a Active Directory environment) you might consider to install the helpful SecretManagement.DpapiNG from Jordan-Borean module and use the following script:

param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true, Position = 0, ValueFromPipeline = $true)][string] $Path,
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true, Position = 1)]$Sid
)
$Item = Get-Item $Path
if ($Item) {
    $OutPath = "$($Item.DirectoryName)\$($Item.BaseName).Protected$($Item.Extension)"
    $ScriptBlock = Get-Content -Raw -Path $Path
    $Base64 = ConvertTo-DpapiNGSecret -InputObject $ScriptBlock -Sid $Sid
    Set-Content -Path $OutPath "`$Base64 = '$Base64'"
    Add-Content -Path $OutPath '$ScriptBlock = ConvertFrom-DpapiNGSecret -InputObject $Base64 -AsString'
    Add-Content -Path $OutPath 'Invoke-Expression $ScriptBlock'
    Add-Content -Path $OutPath 'Remove-Variable Base64, ScriptBlock -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue'
}

Usage:

Install-Module -Name SecretManagement.DpapiNG
.\Protect-Script.ps1 .\MailMessage.ps1 -Sid 'DOMAIN\Domain Admins'

.\MailMessage.Protected.ps1

Q: Accessing css variable in JS file A:

Assuming you're using native CSS variables and not some preprocessor, take a look at this page. At the bottom there's a section called Values in JavaScript which describes how to access native CSS vars in JS code.

getComputedStyle(element).getPropertyValue("--my-var");

However if you are using a CSS preprocessor, it is not possible to retrieve the variables via JS since they're already processed in the build process.

Q: Scatterplot with too many points A:

We can also use contour() from base R (i.e. {graphics}). Extending on what is written here gives

set.seed(1)
X = data.frame(x = rnorm(5000), y = rnorm(5000))
z = MASS::kde2d(X$x, X$y, n = 100)
plot(y~x, data=X, pch = '+', col = "#00000033") # "+" is faster
contour(z, lwd = 2, add = TRUE, col = hcl.colors(10, "YlOrRd", rev=TRUE), labels = FALSE)
contour(z, lwd = 0, add = TRUE, col = "black", labcex = 1.1) # labels in black

Q: Unable to install specific R packages A:

As @konrad-rudolph mentioned in a comment, you missed to install the necessary tools for compiling R packages from source. As described in the R documentation for Windows, you must install the package "RTools".

Beware, however, that your R version 3.6 is quite old. This means that you must go to the archives of the RTools package and install the version for R 3.5.

Q: Connection to MongoDB through my iPhone's personal hotspot A:

Solution: Configure your Mac to use Google or Cloudflare DNS when connected to the iPhone hotspot:

Steps:

  1. System Settings → Network → Select iPhone hotspot connection
  2. Click Details → DNS
  3. Click + and add:
    1. 8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4 (Google DNS)
    2. Or 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1 (Cloudflare)
  4. Click OK and reconnect

After changing DNS settings, you may need to restart your Mac for the changes to take full effect.
